facts.value: within 48 hours of separation or by the next regular payday (not more than 30 days)
facts.summary: South Carolina: when an employee is fired or laid off, final wages are due within 48 hours of separation or by the next regular payday (not more than 30 days).
facts.evidence_quote: When an employer separates an employee from the payroll for any reason, the employer shall pay all wages due to the employee within forty-eight hours of the time of separation or the next regular payday which may not exceed thirty days.

facts.value: within 48 hours of separation or by the next regular payday (not more than 30 days)
facts.summary: South Carolina: when an employee is quits or resigns, final wages are due within 48 hours of separation or by the next regular payday (not more than 30 days).
facts.evidence_quote: Q. If I quit my job, or if I am terminated, does my employer have to pay me all wages due that day? A. No. State law requires the employer to pay an employee all wages due him or her within 48 hours of the day of separation OR the next regularly-scheduled payday, not to exceed 30 days.
facts.source_title: SC LLR Wage and Hour FAQ
facts.source_publisher: South Carolina Department of Labor, Licensing and Regulation

facts.value: No state minimum wage law (federal $7.25 applies to FLSA-covered employers)
facts.applies_to: As listed by U.S. DOL, page updated November 5, 2026
facts.summary: South Carolina basic state minimum wage listed by U.S. DOL: No state minimum wage law (federal $7.25 applies to FLSA-covered employers).
facts.evidence_quote: No state minimum wage law. Employers subject to the Fair Labor Standards Act must pay the current federal minimum wage of $7.25 per hour.
facts.source_title: State Minimum Wage Laws (U.S. DOL Wage and Hour Division)
facts.source_publisher: U.S. Department of Labor, Wage and Hour Division
facts.notes: Local (city or county) minimum wages are not included. Scheduled January 1, 2027 increases are not reflected until DOL updates the page.
